lesson.title: The Double Helix: How DNA Holds Its Shape and Its Secrets
lesson.summary: DNA is a double stranded molecule in which two antiparallel chains of deoxyribonucleotides wind around each other into a helix, held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, a structure that makes DNA both a stable archive and a copyable template.
lesson.body:
DNA is a polymer built from deoxyribonucleotide monomers, each one made of a deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group, and one of four nitrogenous bases: adenine, guanine, cytosine, or thymine. Those nucleotides are linked together through repeated condensation reactions, forming phosphodiester bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next, which builds a long sugar phosphate backbone with a sequence of bases projecting off to one side, exactly as described in the general nucleic acid and nucleotide structure covered earlier.

What makes DNA distinctive is that it does not exist as a single strand, it exists as two strands wound together into a double helix. This structure was famously worked out by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, building on x-ray diffraction data produced by Rosalind Franklin. In the model they proposed, two polynucleotide strands twist around a shared axis in a right-handed double helix, with the sugar phosphate backbones facing outward on either side and the nitrogenous bases pointing inward toward each other. The two strands also run in opposite chemical directions relative to each other, a property called antiparallel, meaning one strand runs 5' to 3' while its partner runs 3' to 5'.

The two strands are held to each other by hydrogen bonds between specific pairs of bases, and this pairing is not random. Adenine always pairs with thymine, connected by two hydrogen bonds, and guanine always pairs with cytosine, connected by three hydrogen bonds. This pattern, known as complementary base pairing, always matches a two-ringed purine with a single-ringed pyrimidine, which keeps the width of the helix constant all the way along its length, since two purines paired together would be too wide and two pyrimidines would be too narrow.

This complementary pairing is not just a structural curiosity, it is what makes DNA copyable. Because the base sequence on one strand fully determines the base sequence needed on its partner strand, each strand can act as a template for building a new complementary strand. During DNA replication, the two original strands separate and each one directs the synthesis of a new partner strand, producing two double helices that are each identical to the original, a process called semiconservative replication. Hydrogen bonds are individually far weaker than the covalent phosphodiester bonds of the backbone, and that difference in strength is exactly what allows enzymes to pry the two strands apart for replication or for reading the gene, without ever having to break the covalent backbone itself.

That same weakness of hydrogen bonds compared to covalent bonds is also why heat can separate, or denature, the two DNA strands without destroying the covalent backbone of either one, a reversible unwinding that laboratory techniques such as PCR rely on directly, and one that echoes the same underlying logic seen earlier when discussing protein denaturation.
